# sysfs_gpio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sysfs_gpio/

## Expand description

GPIO access under Linux using the GPIO sysfs interface

The methods exposed by this library are centered around
the `Pin` struct and map pretty directly the API exposed
by the kernel in syfs [https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Typical usage for systems where one wants to ensure that the pins in use are unexported upon completion looks like the following:

```
use sysfs_gpio::{Direction, Pin};
use std::thread::sleep;
use std::time::Duration;
fn main() {
    let my_led = Pin::new(127); // number depends on chip, etc.
    my_led.with_exported(|| {
        my_led.set_direction(Direction::Out).unwrap();
        loop {
            my_led.set_value(0).unwrap();
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));
            my_led.set_value(1).unwrap();
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));
        }
    }).unwrap();
}
```

# sysfs_gpio 0.6.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sysfs_gpio/latest

# sysfs_gpio

The `sysfs_gpio` crate provides access to the Linux sysfs GPIO interface
([https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt)). It seeks to provide
an API that is safe, convenient, and efficient and supports exporting,
unexporting, reading, writing and waiting for interrupts on pins.

Many devices such as the Raspberry Pi or Beaglebone Black provide userspace access to a number of GPIO peripherals. The standard kernel API for providing access to these GPIOs is via sysfs.

You might want to also check out the
[gpio-utils Project](https://github.com/rust-embedded/gpio-utils) for a
convenient way to associate names with pins and export them as part of system
boot.  That project uses this library.

## Install/Use

To use `sysfs_gpio`, first add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.6"
```
Then, add this to your crate root:

```
use sysfs_gpio;
```
## Example/API

Blinking an LED:

```
use ;
use sleep;
use Duration;
```
More Examples:

- [Blink an LED](https://docs.rs/examples/blinky.rs)
- [Poll a GPIO Input](https://docs.rs/examples/poll.rs)
- [Receive interrupt on GPIO Change](https://docs.rs/examples/interrupt.rs)
- [Poll several pins asynchronously with Tokio](https://docs.rs/examples/tokio.rs)
- [gpio-utils Project (uses most features)](https://github.com/rust-embedded/gpio-utils)

## Features

The following features are planned for the library:

- Support for exporting a GPIO
- Support for unexporting a GPIO
- Support for setting the direction of a GPIO (in/out)
- Support for reading the value of a GPIO input
- Support for writing the value of a GPIO output
- Support for configuring whether a pin is active low/high
- Support for configuring interrupts on GPIO
- Support for polling on GPIO with configured interrupt
-  Support for asynchronous polling using `mio`or`tokio`(requires enabling the`mio-evented`or`async-tokio`crate features, respectively)

## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust 1.65.0 and up.  It *might*
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

## Cross Compiling

Most likely, the machine you are running on is not your development
machine (although it could be).  In those cases, you will need to
cross-compile.  The [rust-cross guide](https://github.com/japaric/rust-cross)
provides excellent, detailed instructions for cross-compiling.

## Running the Example

Cross-compiling can be done by specifying an appropriate target. You can then move that to your device by whatever means and run it.

```
$ cargo build --target=arm-unknown-linux-gnueabihf --example blinky
$ scp target/arm-unknown-linux-gnueabihf/debug/examples/blinky ...
```

# futures - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/futures/^0.3/

## Expand description

Abstractions for asynchronous programming.

This crate provides a number of core abstractions for writing asynchronous code:

- [Futures](https://docs.rs/future/index.html)are single eventual values produced by asynchronous computations. Some programming languages (e.g. JavaScript) call this concept “promise”.
- [Streams](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)represent a series of values produced asynchronously.
- [Sinks](https://docs.rs/sink/index.html)provide support for asynchronous writing of data.
- [Executors](https://docs.rs/executor/index.html)are responsible for running asynchronous tasks.

The crate also contains abstractions for [asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) and
[cross-task communication](https://docs.rs/channel/index.html).

Underlying all of this is the *task system*, which is a form of lightweight
threading. Large asynchronous computations are built up using futures,
streams and sinks, and then spawned as independent tasks that are run to
completion, but *do not block* the thread running them.

The following example describes how the task system context is built and used within macros and keywords such as async and await!.

```
fn main() {
    let pool = ThreadPool::new().expect("Failed to build pool");
    let (tx, rx) = mpsc::unbounded::<i32>();
    // Create a future by an async block, where async is responsible for an
    // implementation of Future. At this point no executor has been provided
    // to this future, so it will not be running.
    let fut_values = async {
        // Create another async block, again where the Future implementation
        // is generated by async. Since this is inside of a parent async block,
        // it will be provided with the executor of the parent block when the parent
        // block is executed.
        //
        // This executor chaining is done by Future::poll whose second argument
        // is a std::task::Context. This represents our executor, and the Future
        // implemented by this async block can be polled using the parent async
        // block's executor.
        let fut_tx_result = async move {
            (0..100).for_each(|v| {
                tx.unbounded_send(v).expect("Failed to send");
            })
        };
        // Use the provided thread pool to spawn the generated future
        // responsible for transmission
        pool.spawn_ok(fut_tx_result);
        let fut_values = rx
            .map(|v| v * 2)
            .collect();
        // Use the executor provided to this async block to wait for the
        // future to complete.
        fut_values.await
    };
    // Actually execute the above future, which will invoke Future::poll and
    // subsequently chain appropriate Future::poll and methods needing executors
    // to drive all futures. Eventually fut_values will be driven to completion.
    let values: Vec<i32> = executor::block_on(fut_values);
    println!("Values={:?}", values);
}
```
The majority of examples and code snippets in this crate assume that they are inside an async block as written above.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [join](https://docs.rs/macro.join.html)- `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, returning a tuple of all results once complete.
- [pending](https://docs.rs/macro.pending.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which yields to the event loop once.
- [pin_mut](https://docs.rs/macro.pin_mut.html)
- Pins a value on the stack.
- [poll](https://docs.rs/macro.poll.html)- `async-await`
- A macro which returns the result of polling a future once within the
current `async`context.
- [ready](https://docs.rs/macro.ready.html)
- Extracts the successful type of `Poll<T>`.
- [select](https://docs.rs/macro.select.html)- `async-await`and- `std`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. If multiple futures are ready,
one will be pseudo-randomly selected at runtime. Futures directly
passed to `select!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [select_](https://docs.rs/macro.select_biased.html)- biased - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures and streams simultaneously, executing the branch
for the future that finishes first. Unlike `select!``select_biased!`must be`Unpin`and implement`FusedFuture`.
- [stream_](https://docs.rs/macro.stream_select.html)- select - `async-await`and- `std`
- Combines several streams, all producing the same `Item`type, into one stream. This is similar to`select_all`but does not require the streams to all be the same type. It also keeps the streams inline, and does not require`Box<dyn Stream>`s to be allocated. Streams passed to this macro must be`Unpin`.
- [try_](https://docs.rs/macro.try_join.html)- join - `async-await`
- Polls multiple futures simultaneously, resolving to a `Result`

# mio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mio/^0.8/

## Expand description

Mio is a fast, low-level I/O library for Rust focusing on non-blocking APIs and event notification for building high performance I/O apps with as little overhead as possible over the OS abstractions.

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

Using Mio starts by creating a [ Poll](https://docs.rs/mio/struct.Poll.html), which reads events from the OS and
puts them into

[. You can handle I/O events from the OS with it.](https://docs.rs/mio/event/struct.Events.html)

`Events`For more detail, see [ Poll](https://docs.rs/mio/struct.Poll.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Examples can found in the `examples` directory of the source code, or [on
GitHub](https://github.com/tokio-rs/mio/tree/master/examples).

[§](https://docs.rs#guide)Guide

A getting started guide is available in the [ guide](https://docs.rs/guide/index.html) module.

[§](https://docs.rs#available-features)Available features

The available features are described in the [ features](https://docs.rs/features/index.html) module.

# tokio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/tokio/^1/

## Expand description

A runtime for writing reliable network applications without compromising speed.

Tokio is an event-driven, non-blocking I/O platform for writing asynchronous applications with the Rust programming language. At a high level, it provides a few major components:

- Tools for [working with asynchronous tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks), including[synchronization primitives and channels](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html)and[timeouts, sleeps, and intervals](https://docs.rs/time/index.html).
- APIs for [performing asynchronous I/O](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io), including[TCP and UDP](https://docs.rs/net/index.html)sockets,[filesystem](https://docs.rs/fs/index.html)operations, and[process](https://docs.rs/process/index.html)and[signal](https://docs.rs/signal/index.html)management.
- A [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)for executing asynchronous code, including a task scheduler, an I/O driver backed by the operating system’s event queue (`epoll`,`kqueue`,`IOCP`, etc…), and a high performance timer.

Guide level documentation is found on the [website](https://tokio.rs/tokio/tutorial).

[§](https://docs.rs#a-tour-of-tokio)A Tour of Tokio

Tokio consists of a number of modules that provide a range of functionality essential for implementing asynchronous applications in Rust. In this section, we will take a brief tour of Tokio, summarizing the major APIs and their uses.

The easiest way to get started is to enable all features. Do this by
enabling the `full` feature flag:

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#authoring-applications)Authoring applications

Tokio is great for writing applications and most users in this case shouldn’t
worry too much about what features they should pick. If you’re unsure, we suggest
going with `full` to ensure that you don’t run into any road blocks while you’re
building your application.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

This example shows the quickest way to get started with Tokio.

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["full"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#authoring-libraries)Authoring libraries

As a library author your goal should be to provide the lightest weight crate that is based on Tokio. To achieve this you should ensure that you only enable the features you need. This allows users to pick up your crate without having to enable unnecessary features.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

This example shows how you may want to import features for a library that just
needs to `tokio::spawn` and use a `TcpStream`.

`tokio = { version = "1", features = ["rt", "net"] }`[§](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks)Working With Tasks

Asynchronous programs in Rust are based around lightweight, non-blocking
units of execution called [ tasks](https://docs.rs#working-with-tasks). The

[module provides important tools for working with tasks:](https://docs.rs/task/index.html)

`tokio::task`- The `spawn``JoinHandle`
- Functions for [running blocking operations](https://docs.rs/task/index.html#blocking-and-yielding)in an asynchronous task context.

The [ tokio::task](https://docs.rs/task/index.html) module is present only when the “rt” feature flag
is enabled.

The [ tokio::sync](https://docs.rs/sync/index.html) module contains synchronization primitives to use when
needing to communicate or share data. These include:

- channels (`oneshot``mpsc``watch``broadcast`
- a non-blocking `Mutex`
- an asynchronous `Barrier`

The `tokio::sync` module is present only when the “sync” feature flag is
enabled.

The [ tokio::time](https://docs.rs/time/index.html) module provides utilities for tracking time and
scheduling work. This includes functions for setting

[timeouts](https://docs.rs/time/fn.timeout.html)for tasks,

[sleeping](https://docs.rs/time/fn.sleep.html)work to run in the future, or

[repeating an operation at an interval](https://docs.rs/time/fn.interval.html).

In order to use `tokio::time`, the “time” feature flag must be enabled.

Finally, Tokio provides a *runtime* for executing asynchronous tasks. Most
applications can use the [ #[tokio::main]](https://docs.rs/attr.main.html) macro to run their code on the
Tokio runtime. However, this macro provides only basic configuration options. As
an alternative, the

[module provides more powerful APIs for configuring and managing runtimes. You should use that module if the](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)

`tokio::runtime``#[tokio::main]` macro doesn’t
provide the functionality you need.Using the runtime requires the “rt” or “rt-multi-thread” feature flags, to
enable the current-thread [single-threaded scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#current-thread-scheduler) and the [multi-thread
scheduler](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#multi-thread-scheduler), respectively. See the [ runtime module
documentation](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html#runtime-scheduler) for details. In addition, the “macros” feature
flag enables the

`#[tokio::main]` and `#[tokio::test]` attributes.[§](https://docs.rs#cpu-bound-tasks-and-blocking-code)CPU-bound tasks and blocking code

Tokio is able to concurrently run many tasks on a few threads by repeatedly
swapping the currently running task on each thread. However, this kind of
swapping can only happen at `.await` points, so code that spends a long time
without reaching an `.await` will prevent other tasks from running. To
combat this, Tokio provides two kinds of threads: Core threads and blocking threads.

The core threads are where all asynchronous code runs, and Tokio will by default
spawn one for each CPU core. You can use the environment variable `TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS`
to override the default value.

The blocking threads are spawned on demand, can be used to run blocking code
that would otherwise block other tasks from running and are kept alive when
not used for a certain amount of time which can be configured with [ thread_keep_alive](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.Builder.html#method.thread_keep_alive).
Since it is not possible for Tokio to swap out blocking tasks, like it
can do with asynchronous code, the upper limit on the number of blocking
threads is very large. These limits can be configured on the

[.](https://docs.rs/runtime/struct.Builder.html)

`Builder`To spawn a blocking task, you should use the [ spawn_blocking](https://docs.rs/task/fn.spawn_blocking.html) function.

```
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() {
    // This is running on a core thread.
    let blocking_task = tokio::task::spawn_blocking(|| {
        // This is running on a blocking thread.
        // Blocking here is ok.
    });
    // We can wait for the blocking task like this:
    // If the blocking task panics, the unwrap below will propagate the
    // panic.
    blocking_task.await.unwrap();
}
```
If your code is CPU-bound and you wish to limit the number of threads used
to run it, you should use a separate thread pool dedicated to CPU bound tasks.
For example, you could consider using the [rayon](https://docs.rs/rayon) library for CPU-bound
tasks. It is also possible to create an extra Tokio runtime dedicated to
CPU-bound tasks, but if you do this, you should be careful that the extra
runtime runs *only* CPU-bound tasks, as IO-bound tasks on that runtime
will behave poorly.

Hint: If using rayon, you can use a [ oneshot](https://docs.rs/sync/oneshot/index.html) channel to send the result back
to Tokio when the rayon task finishes.

[§](https://docs.rs#asynchronous-io)Asynchronous IO

As well as scheduling and running tasks, Tokio provides everything you need to perform input and output asynchronously.

The [ tokio::io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html) module provides Tokio’s asynchronous core I/O primitives,
the

[,](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncRead.html)

`AsyncRead`[, and](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncWrite.html)

`AsyncWrite`[traits. In addition, when the “io-util” feature flag is enabled, it also provides combinators and functions for working with these traits, forming as an asynchronous counterpart to](https://docs.rs/io/trait.AsyncBufRead.html)

`AsyncBufRead`[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/io/index.html)

`std::io`Tokio also includes APIs for performing various kinds of I/O and interacting with the operating system asynchronously. These include:

- `tokio::net`- [TCP](https://docs.rs/net/tcp/index.html),- [UDP](https://docs.rs/net/struct.UdpSocket.html), and- [Unix Domain Sockets](https://docs.rs/net/unix/index.html)(enabled by the “net” feature flag),
- `tokio::fs`- `std::fs`
- `tokio::signal`
- `tokio::process`

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

A simple TCP echo server:

```
use tokio::net::TcpListener;
use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};
#[tokio::main]
async fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let listener = TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:8080").await?;
    loop {
        let (mut socket, _) = listener.accept().await?;
        tokio::spawn(async move {
            let mut buf = [0; 1024];
            // In a loop, read data from the socket and write the data back.
            loop {
                let n = match socket.read(&mut buf).await {
                    // socket closed
                    Ok(0) => return,
                    Ok(n) => n,
                    Err(e) => {
                        eprintln!("failed to read from socket; err = {:?}", e);
                        return;
                    }
                };
                // Write the data back
                if let Err(e) = socket.write_all(&buf[0..n]).await {
                    eprintln!("failed to write to socket; err = {:?}", e);
                    return;
                }
            }
        });
    }
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

Tokio uses a set of [feature flags](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html#the-features-section) to reduce the amount of compiled code. It
is possible to just enable certain features over others. By default, Tokio
does not enable any features but allows one to enable a subset for their use
case. Below is a list of the available feature flags. You may also notice
above each function, struct and trait there is listed one or more feature flags
that are required for that item to be used. If you are new to Tokio it is
recommended that you use the `full` feature flag which will enable all public APIs.
Beware though that this will pull in many extra dependencies that you may not
need.

- `full`: Enables all features listed below except- `test-util`and unstable features.
- `rt`: Enables- `tokio::spawn`, the current-thread scheduler, and non-scheduler utilities.
- `rt-multi-thread`: Enables the heavier, multi-threaded, work-stealing scheduler.
- `io-util`: Enables the IO based- `Ext`traits.
- `io-std`: Enable- `Stdout`,- `Stdin`and- `Stderr`types.
- `net`: Enables- `tokio::net`types such as- `TcpStream`,- `UnixStream`and- `UdpSocket`, as well as (on Unix-like systems)- `AsyncFd`and (on FreeBSD)- `PollAio`.
- `time`: Enables- `tokio::time`types and allows the schedulers to enable the built-in timer.
- `process`: Enables- `tokio::process`types.
- `macros`: Enables- `#[tokio::main]`and- `#[tokio::test]`macros.
- `sync`: Enables all- `tokio::sync`types.
- `signal`: Enables all- `tokio::signal`types.
- `fs`: Enables- `tokio::fs`types.
- `test-util`: Enables testing based infrastructure for the Tokio runtime.
- `parking_lot`: As a potential optimization, use the- `parking_lot`- `const`context.- `MSRV`may increase according to the- `parking_lot`

*Note:  AsyncRead and AsyncWrite traits do not require any features and are
always available.*

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-features)Unstable features

Some feature flags are only available when specifying the `tokio_unstable` flag:

- `tracing`: Enables tracing events.
- `io-uring`: Enables- `io-uring`(Linux only).
- `taskdump`: Enables- `taskdump`(Linux only).

Likewise, this flag enables access to unstable APIs.

This flag enables **unstable** features. The public API of these features
may break in 1.x releases. To enable these features, the `--cfg tokio_unstable` argument must be passed to `rustc` when compiling. This
serves to explicitly opt-in to features which may break semver conventions,
since Cargo [does not yet directly support such opt-ins](https://internals.rust-lang.org/t/feature-request-unstable-opt-in-non-transitive-crate-features/16193#why-not-a-crate-feature-2).

You can specify it in your project’s `.cargo/config.toml` file:

```
[build]
rustflags = ["--cfg", "tokio_unstable"]
```
`[build]` section does **not**go in a

`Cargo.toml` file. Instead it must be placed in the Cargo config
file `.cargo/config.toml`.
Alternatively, you can specify it with an environment variable:

```
## Many *nix shells:
export RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"
cargo build
```
```
## Windows PowerShell:
$Env:RUSTFLAGS="--cfg tokio_unstable"
cargo build
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-platforms)Supported platforms

Tokio currently guarantees support for the following platforms:

- Linux
- Windows
- Android (API level 21)
- macOS
- iOS
- FreeBSD

Tokio will continue to support these platforms in the future. However, future releases may change requirements such as the minimum required libc version on Linux, the API level on Android, or the supported FreeBSD release.

Beyond the above platforms, Tokio is intended to work on all platforms
supported by the mio crate. You can find a longer list [in mio’s
documentation](https://crates.io/crates/mio#platforms). However, these additional platforms may
become unsupported in the future.

Note that Wine is considered to be a different platform from Windows. See mio’s documentation for more information on Wine support.

[§](https://docs.rs#wasm-support)`WASM` support

Tokio has some limited support for the `WASM` platform. Without the
`tokio_unstable` flag, the following features are supported:

- `sync`
- `macros`
- `io-util`
- `rt`
- `time`

Enabling any other feature (including `full`) will cause a compilation
failure.

The `time` module will only work on `WASM` platforms that have support for
timers (e.g. wasm32-wasi). The timing functions will panic if used on a `WASM`
platform that does not support timers.

Note also that if the runtime becomes indefinitely idle, it will panic immediately instead of blocking forever. On platforms that don’t support time, this means that the runtime can never be idle in any way.

[§](https://docs.rs#unstable-wasm-support)Unstable `WASM` support

Tokio also has unstable support for some additional `WASM` features. This
requires the use of the `tokio_unstable` flag.

Using this flag enables the use of `tokio::net` on the wasm32-wasi target.
However, not all methods are available on the networking types as `WASI`
currently does not support the creation of new sockets from within `WASM`.
Because of this, sockets must currently be created via the `FromRawFd`
trait.

# sysfs_gpio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sysfs_gpio/latest/target-redirect/sysfs_gpio/

## Expand description

GPIO access under Linux using the GPIO sysfs interface

The methods exposed by this library are centered around
the `Pin` struct and map pretty directly the API exposed
by the kernel in syfs [https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Typical usage for systems where one wants to ensure that the pins in use are unexported upon completion looks like the following:

```
use sysfs_gpio::{Direction, Pin};
use std::thread::sleep;
use std::time::Duration;
fn main() {
    let my_led = Pin::new(127); // number depends on chip, etc.
    my_led.with_exported(|| {
        my_led.set_direction(Direction::Out).unwrap();
        loop {
            my_led.set_value(0).unwrap();
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));
            my_led.set_value(1).unwrap();
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));
        }
    }).unwrap();
}
```

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# datum - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/datum-core/0.9.0/datum/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#datum)Datum

🪼 - Just “Stream” anything :]

Datum is a Rust stream processing library scaffolded around Ractor actors and a push-based stream abstraction. The compatibility target is Akka/Pekko Streams Typed API shape and behavior, with Rust-native ownership, async, and benchmarking constraints.

[§](https://docs.rs#install)Install

Add Datum to your project from crates.io:

`cargo add datum-core`Or in `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
datum-core = "0.9"
```

Note:The package is published as`datum-core`(the name`datum`is taken on crates.io), but the import path stays`use datum::…`— the crate’s library name is`datum`.

To track an unreleased commit instead:

```
[dependencies]
datum-core = { git = "https://github.com/Aethergrids/Datum", tag = "v0.9.0" }
```
[§](https://docs.rs#upstream-references)Upstream References

- Ractor crate: `0.15.13`
- Optional Ractor cluster crate: `0.15.13`, enabled with`--features cluster`
- Akka source submodule: `third_party/akka`, tracking upstream`main`and pinned in this repository at commit`58f1f6db2e505e87f5dc115ee9476833872e7ae0`
- Latest stable Akka tag observed during setup: `v2.10.18`

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-highlights-v090)Feature highlights (v0.9.0)

- **Concurrency primitives**(- `datum::concurrent`) —- `Signal<T>`(latest-value state cell with a lock-free- `get()`and a coalesced change feed),- `Subscription<T>`(the same state cell with a lossless every-change feed),- `Channel<T>`(closeable bounded MPSC), and- `Topic<T>`(pub-sub broadcast with backpressure/sliding/dropping overflow policies). Benchmarked 4-way against FS2, ZIO, and Akka: every row beats the best JVM competitor on both wall-clock and CPU.
- **API ergonomics (additive, zero semantic change)**—- `use datum::prelude::*;`, terminal shortcuts (- `run_fold`/- `run_foreach`/- `run_reduce`),- `(0..n).into_source()`/- `Source::from(vec)`, the graph wiring DSL- `builder.wire(a.to(&b))`(with- `connect()`still first-class), and idiomatic- `try_*`fallible operators (- `try_map`,- `try_filter`, … —- `*_result`names deprecated).
- **Complete Akka Streams surface**— the linear DSL, GraphDSL with typed junctions and cycles, substreams, dynamic streams (kill switches, hubs), StreamRefs (same-process splice + remote transport via- `datum-net`), streaming IO, and IO adapters bridging to- `std::io::Read`/- `Write`.
- `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`on the- `datum`crate itself; lock-free internals come from safe deps (- `crossbeam-queue`,- `arc-swap`).

[§](https://docs.rs#development)Development

```
cargo test
cargo check --benches
cargo bench --bench push_baseline
cargo bench --bench source_flow
cargo bench --bench materialization
cargo bench --bench graph
cargo bench --bench actor_ask
benches/actor_ask_compare/run.sh
```
```
use datum::prelude::*;
let sum = (0_u64..1_000)
    .into_source()
    .map(|item| item + 1)
    .filter(|item| item % 2 == 0)
    .run_fold(0_u64, |acc, item| acc + item)
    .unwrap()
    .wait()
    .unwrap();
assert_eq!(sum, 250_500);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#benchmarks)Benchmarks

Datum is benchmarked head-to-head against warmed Akka/Pekko Streams across eight core areas —
Source/Flow, materialization, graph/junctions, actor ask, dynamic streams, streaming IO, substreams,
and queues — plus network carriers (`datum-net`) and a 4-way concurrency-primitives comparison
against FS2, ZIO, and Akka. Honest per-path numbers (including any at-parity rows) are in the result
tables under `roadmap/benchmarks/`. The harness adds a `Datum CPU us/op` column on purpose: some
wins come partly from busy-spinning while a JVM parks — a real cost the wall-clock number hides.

Qualitative summary of the current state:

- **Fused linear path:**13–46x Akka (typed plan; all common sink shapes).
- **Junctions:**2.3–340x; typed kernels cover all major shapes;- **graph cycles**~29x.
- **Concurrency primitives (vs best of FS2/ZIO/Akka per row):**Channel MPSC ×1024 7.5x wall / 20.5x CPU; Signal reads ~ns-class (3.6–7.8x ZIO); Signal propagation ×1024 83x; Subscription lossless ×256 43x; Topic fanout ×1024 23x.
- **Remote StreamRefs (forced-remote Akka Artery-TCP, fair):**~9.9x faster wall, ~14.8x lower CPU, ~35x lower allocation; same-process splice ~6.5x.
- **Dynamic hubs:**MergeHub p16 ~16x (p1 ~0.46x — core materialization floor, documented); BroadcastHub 1.3–2x; PartitionHub 1.4–2.7x.
- **Queues:**source-queue backpressure ~985x; bounded queue ~parity wall with ~112x less allocation.
- **Actor ask:**~2.4–3x at p2–p4; allocation dominated by upstream Ractor boxing (~848 B/element, upstream-blocked).
- **Streaming IO adapters:**~7.4x on the round-trip scenario;- **materialization:**at parity.

Run a comparison (requires a JDK + `sbt`); each runner writes a rendered table under `target/<area>-comparison/`:

```
benches/source_flow_compare/run.sh
benches/materialization_compare/run.sh
benches/graph_compare/run.sh
benches/actor_ask_compare/run.sh
benches/dynamic_streams_compare/run.sh
benches/streaming_io_compare/run.sh
benches/substreams_compare/run.sh
```
Current result tables, the per-operator coverage matrix, and apples-to-apples caveats:

- `roadmap/benchmarks/source-flow.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/materialization.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/graph.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/actor-ask.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/dynamic-streams.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/streaming-io.md`
- `roadmap/benchmarks/substreams.md`
- `roadmap/M1-v0.1.0-foundation.md`— coverage matrix, optimization status & apples-to-apples caveats
- `roadmap/M4-v0.4.0-completeness-hardening.md`— M4 work packages and exit criteria

See [ roadmap/](https://docs.rs/roadmap/README.md) for the full milestone roadmap. User documentation is the published VitePress site (Cloudflare Pages);

`docs/` holds its source. `roadmap/` holds internal planning and benchmark records.## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [actor](https://docs.rs/actor/index.html)
- Actor interop: Ractor-backed stream bridges plus the remote StreamRefs seam.
- [concurrent](https://docs.rs/concurrent/index.html)
- Stream-native concurrency primitives.
- [context](https://docs.rs/context/index.html)
- Context-aware stream wrappers.
- [dynamic](https://docs.rs/dynamic/index.html)
- Dynamic stream controls and attachment points modeled after Akka Streams.
- [graph](https://docs.rs/graph/index.html)
- Runtime-checked graph, shape, port, and junction primitives.
- [io](https://docs.rs/io/index.html)
- Streaming I/O — file and TCP sources/sinks, byte framing, compression, and `std::io`bridges.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- [queue](https://docs.rs/queue/index.html)
- Bounded and unbounded queues that bridge external producers into a Datum stream.
- [stream](https://docs.rs/stream/index.html)
- The linear Source/Flow/Sink DSL and the runtime that materializes it — Datum’s primary public surface, mirroring Akka/Pekko Streams Typed.
- [testkit](https://docs.rs/testkit/index.html)
- Stream testing probes built on Datum’s normal runtime.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Actor](https://docs.rs/struct.ActorRef.html)- Ref
- An [ActorRef](https://docs.rs/struct.ActorRef.html)is a strongly-typed wrapper over an[ActorCell](https://docs.rs/ractor/0.15.13/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/ractor/actor/actor_cell/struct.ActorCell.html)to provide some syntactic wrapping on the requirement to pass the actor’s message type everywhere.
- [Attributes](https://docs.rs/struct.Attributes.html)
- An ordered, immutable collection of `Attribute`

# lellm - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lellm/0.4.6/lellm/

## Expand description

LeLLM — Rust LLM orchestration framework.

默认开启 `provider`（core + provider 适配层）。

```
# 默认：core + provider
lellm = "0.2"
# 需要 Graph 编排层
lellm = { version = "0.2", features = ["graph"] }
# 需要 Agent 运行时
lellm = { version = "0.2", features = ["agent"] }
# 需要 MCP 协议
lellm = { version = "0.2", features = ["mcp"] }
# 全部启用
lellm = { version = "0.2", features = ["full"] }
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [lellm_provider](https://docs.rs/lellm-provider/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lellm_provider/index.html)as provider;

---

# lellm_derive - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lellm-derive/0.4.6/lellm_derive/

## Expand description

lellm-derive — 派生宏与属性宏。

[§](https://docs.rs#%E4%B8%89%E7%BA%A7-api)三级 API

[§](https://docs.rs#level-1-tool-%E5%87%BD%E6%95%B0%E5%AE%8F%E6%8E%A8%E8%8D%9095-%E7%94%A8%E6%88%B7)Level 1: `#[tool]` 函数宏（推荐，95% 用户）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::ToolResult;
use lellm_derive::tool;
#[tool(name = "search", description = "搜索互联网信息")]
async fn search(query: String, limit: Option<u32>) -> ToolResult {
    // 实现逻辑
    Ok(format!("搜索结果: {}", query))
}
// 无依赖 — 直接调用生成的工厂函数：
builder.tool(search_tool());
// 有依赖 — 使用 _with 后缀工厂函数：
let client = SearchClient::new();
builder.tool(search_tool_with({
    let client = client.clone();
    move |args| async move {
        client.search(&args.query, args.limit).await
    }
}));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#level-2-derivetool-struct-%E5%AE%8F%E9%AB%98%E7%BA%A7%E7%94%A8%E6%88%B7)Level 2: `#[derive(Tool)]` struct 宏（高级用户）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::ToolResult;
use lellm_derive::Tool;
#[derive(Tool, JsonSchema)]
#[tool(name = "search", description = "搜索互联网信息")]
struct SearchArgs {
    /// 搜索关键词
    query: String,
    /// 返回数量
    limit: Option<u32>,
}
// 注册：
let reg = SearchArgs::safe(|args| async move {
    Ok(format!("搜索结果: {}", args.query))
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#level-3-toolregistrationsafe%E6%A1%86%E6%9E%B6%E5%BC%80%E5%8F%91%E8%80%85)Level 3: `ToolRegistration::safe()`（框架开发者）

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use lellm_agent::{ToolDefinition, ToolRegistration};
let reg = ToolRegistration::safe(
    ToolDefinition {
        name: "search".to_string(),
        description: "搜索".to_string(),
        parameters: serde_json::json!({
            "type": "object",
            "properties": { "query": { "type": "string" } }
        }),
    },
    |args| async { Ok(args["query"].as_str().unwrap().to_string()) }
);
```

# mermaid_rs_renderer - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/mermaid-rs-renderer/0.3.0/mermaid_rs_renderer/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#mmdr---fast-mermaid-diagram-renderer)mmdr - Fast Mermaid Diagram Renderer

A pure Rust implementation of Mermaid diagram rendering, providing 100-600x faster rendering than mermaid-cli by eliminating browser dependencies.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{render, render_with_options, RenderOptions};
let diagram = r#"
flowchart LR
    A[Start] --> B{Decision}
    B -->|Yes| C[OK]
    B -->|No| D[Cancel]
"#;
// Simple one-liner
let svg = render(diagram).unwrap();
// With options
let svg = render_with_options(diagram, RenderOptions::default()).unwrap();
```
[§](https://docs.rs#pipeline-control)Pipeline Control

For more control over the rendering pipeline, use the individual stages:

```
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{parse_mermaid, compute_layout, render_svg};
use mermaid_rs_renderer::{Theme, LayoutConfig};
let diagram = "flowchart LR; A-->B-->C";
// Stage 1: Parse
let parsed = parse_mermaid(diagram).unwrap();
// Stage 2: Layout
let theme = Theme::modern();
let config = LayoutConfig::default();
let layout = compute_layout(&parsed.graph, &theme, &config);
// Stage 3: Render
let svg = render_svg(&layout, &theme, &config);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#supported-diagram-types)Supported Diagram Types

- **Flowcharts**(- `flowchart`/- `graph`): TD, TB, LR, RL, BT directions
- **Sequence Diagrams**(- `sequenceDiagram`)
- **Class Diagrams**(- `classDiagram`)
- **State Diagrams**(- `stateDiagram-v2`)
- **ER Diagrams**(- `erDiagram`)
- **Pie Charts**(- `pie`)
- **XY Charts**(- `xychart`)
- **Quadrant Charts**(- `quadrantChart`)
- **Gantt**(- `gantt`)
- **Timeline**(- `timeline`)
- **Journey**(- `journey`)
- **Mindmap**(- `mindmap`)
- **Git Graph**(- `gitGraph`)

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Pure Rust, no browser or Node.js required
- ~3ms cold start vs ~2500ms for mermaid-cli
- ~15MB memory vs ~300MB for mermaid-cli
- SVG and PNG output (PNG via resvg)
- Customizable themes and layout configuration

[§](https://docs.rs#cargo-features)Cargo Features

- `cli`
- `png`

For minimal dependencies (e.g., embedding in other tools like Zola):

```
[dependencies]
mermaid-rs-renderer = { version = "0.2.2", default-features = false }
```

# trifle - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/trifle/0.5.0/trifle/

## Expand description

`trifle` — embedded, typo-tolerant trigram fuzzy search backed by SQLite.

trifle indexes short text segments and answers typo- and partial-tolerant queries, returning
matches that each carry where they matched. It owns a single SQLite store holding the segment
text, the caller key, and an inverted index (a base-plus-delta CRoaring posting per token),
and ranks by rarity-weighted shared-token overlap, counted bit-sliced in the
[ trifle_overlap](https://docs.rs/trifle-overlap/0.5.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/trifle_overlap/index.html) engine. The store is a derived, rebuildable cache over a caller-owned
source of truth; trifle never touches the caller’s data store.

It targets large corpora of small documents (≲ 1–2 KB per segment) read often and written infrequently. It is a fuzzy lexical overlap engine: rarer shared grams weigh more, and rarity is normalized per script class so a CJK bigram and a Latin trigram compare fairly. There is no BM25 or relevance tier.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick start

```
use trifle::{Config, Index, Schema, SearchOpts};
let dir = tempfile::tempdir().unwrap();
let index = Index::open_at(&dir.path().join("trifle.db"), Schema::flat(), Config::default())?;
// Writes go through a short-lived writer lease; commit makes them durable + visible.
let mut w = index.writer()?;
w.upsert(1, &[("front", "the quick brown fox")])?;
w.upsert(2, &[("front", "the quack brown ox")])?;
w.commit()?;
drop(w);
// Reads go through a reader lease. A typo'd query still matches.
let hits = index.reader()?.matches("quikc brown", &SearchOpts::new(), 10)?;
assert!(hits.iter().any(|m| m.key.as_i64() == Some(1)));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-data-model)The data model

A [ Schema](https://docs.rs/struct.Schema.html) declares a

**key**(its shape —

`Integer`/`Text`/`Blob`) plus named **text fields**. A

[is a](https://docs.rs/struct.Document.html)

`Document`[and a set of named segments (](https://docs.rs/enum.Key.html)

`Key``label → text`); a match
comes back as a [carrying the document key, the matched segment’s label, the matched byte span, and the segment’s text. There is no](https://docs.rs/struct.Match.html)

`Match``doc` table: the key lives directly on each
segment row.[§](https://docs.rs#the-read-surface)The read surface

[ Reader::matches](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html#method.matches) is the eager default: the top

`limit` hydrated matches.
[is the lazy spine: a best-first](https://docs.rs/struct.Reader.html#method.candidates)

`Reader::candidates`[of provenance-only](https://docs.rs/struct.CandidateStream.html)

`CandidateStream`[s that a caller composes reranking, pagination, or fusion over, hydrating only what it keeps. Filtering is the opt-in](https://docs.rs/struct.Candidate.html)

`Candidate`[over the caller’s live data.](https://docs.rs/struct.SqlFilter.html)

`SqlFilter`[§](https://docs.rs#ingest-and-maintenance)Ingest and maintenance

Writes are cheap (a small delta append) and visible after [ commit](https://docs.rs/struct.Writer.html#method.commit).

[folds pending deltas;](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html#method.compact)

`compact`[is the signal that a compaction is due.](https://docs.rs/struct.Stats.html#structfield.delta_backlog)

`Stats::delta_backlog`[fully reindexes via an atomic shadow swap, which a tokenizer,](https://docs.rs/struct.Index.html#method.rebuild)

`rebuild``data_version`, or schema change requires (each drops the cache on open).## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [error](https://docs.rs/error/index.html)
- The crate error type.

# sandpit - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sandpit/0.5.3/sandpit/

## Expand description

A concurrent, generational, trace and sweep garbage collected arena.

[§](https://docs.rs#creating-an-arena)Creating An Arena

All garbage collection in Sandpit happens within an arena. Therefore, to be begin we can start with creating a new arena.

This can be done like so..

```
use sandpit::{Arena, Root};
// This creates an arena with a `MyRoot` as the root.
let gc: Arena<Root![MyRoot]> = Arena::new(|mutator| {
    MyRoot::new(mutator)
});
```
There are two big things to unpack here:

- An `Arena`is generic on its single Root value which it holds.
- The Root of an `Arena`must be a Higher Kinded Type(HKT).

This is explained in much further depth in [ sandpit::Arena](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#trace-trait)Trace Trait

For a type to be GC’ed it is required to impl [ Trace](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)
which can be safely derived as long as all inner types also impl

[.](https://docs.rs/trait.Trace.html)

`Trace````
use sandpit::{Trace, Gc, GcOpt};
#[derive(Trace)]
enum Value<'gc> {
    // GC values must be branded with a mutation lifetime
    // to ensure freeing memory can happen safely.
    A(Gc<'gc, A>), // Mutable pointer to a garbage collected value
    B(GcOpt<'gc, B>), // Optionally null pointer that is also mutable. Can be unwrapped into a Gc.
}
// All inner values must be trace, therefore types A and B must impl Trace as well.
```
Essentially when a value is traced the tracer will mark the value as live, and call trace on all its inner pointers to GC values.

There are 2 types of GC pointers:

A type may also derive [ TraceLeaf](https://docs.rs/trait.TraceLeaf.html), if it contains no GC pointers.

[allows for easier interior mutability.](https://docs.rs/trait.TraceLeaf.html)

`TraceLeaf`[§](https://docs.rs#mutating-the-arena)Mutating the Arena

Once you have your arena and your traceable types, you can begin allocating
them in the arena by calling [ Arena::mutate](https://docs.rs/struct.Arena.html#method.mutate). Within a mutation
we can essentially do 3 important things:

- Access all data reaachable from the root.
- Create new garbage collected values.
- Update Gc pointers to point to new values via a `WriteBarrier`

```
use sandpit::{Trace, Gc};
arena.mutate(|mutator, root| {
    // We can access everything reachable from the root.
    traverse(root);
    // We can allocate new Gc values.
    // Here is a pointer, to a pointer, to a bool!
    let gc_mut = Gc::new(mutator,
        Gc::new(mutator, true)
    );
    // We can mutate existing inner Gc and GcOpt pointers.
    gc_mut.write_barrier(mutator, |barrier| {
        barrier.set(Gc::new(mutator, false));
    })
});
```
[§](https://docs.rs#collection-and-yielding)Collection and Yielding

In order for the Gc to free memory, and do so safely, all mutations must exit. Therefore, if a mutation involves a continuous loop of instructions, it must exit it’s mutation every so often to allow the GC to free memory.

The mutator exposes a signal([ Mutator::gc_yield](https://docs.rs/struct.Mutator.html#method.gc_yield)) which indicates if it is ready to free memory,
and that the mutation should end.

```
arena.mutate(|mutator, root| loop {
    // during this function it is likely the the GC will concurrently begin tracing!
    allocate_stuff(mutator, root);
    if mutator.gc_yield() {
        // the mutator is signaling to us that memory is ready to be freed so we should leave the mutation context
        break;
    } else {
        // if the mutator isn't signaling for us to yield then we
        // are fine to go on allocating more garbage
    }
});
```
* WARNING:* If a mutation continously runs without occasionally checking
the yield signal, memory cannot be freed!

# sysfs_gpio 0.6.2 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sysfs_gpio/0.6.2

# sysfs_gpio

The `sysfs_gpio` crate provides access to the Linux sysfs GPIO interface
([https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt)). It seeks to provide
an API that is safe, convenient, and efficient and supports exporting,
unexporting, reading, writing and waiting for interrupts on pins.

Many devices such as the Raspberry Pi or Beaglebone Black provide userspace access to a number of GPIO peripherals. The standard kernel API for providing access to these GPIOs is via sysfs.

You might want to also check out the
[gpio-utils Project](https://github.com/rust-embedded/gpio-utils) for a
convenient way to associate names with pins and export them as part of system
boot.  That project uses this library.

## Install/Use

To use `sysfs_gpio`, first add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.6"
```
Then, add this to your crate root:

```
use sysfs_gpio;
```
## Example/API

Blinking an LED:

```
use ;
use sleep;
use Duration;
```
More Examples:

- [Blink an LED](https://docs.rs/examples/blinky.rs)
- [Poll a GPIO Input](https://docs.rs/examples/poll.rs)
- [Receive interrupt on GPIO Change](https://docs.rs/examples/interrupt.rs)
- [Poll several pins asynchronously with Tokio](https://docs.rs/examples/tokio.rs)
- [gpio-utils Project (uses most features)](https://github.com/rust-embedded/gpio-utils)

## Features

The following features are planned for the library:

- Support for exporting a GPIO
- Support for unexporting a GPIO
- Support for setting the direction of a GPIO (in/out)
- Support for reading the value of a GPIO input
- Support for writing the value of a GPIO output
- Support for configuring whether a pin is active low/high
- Support for configuring interrupts on GPIO
- Support for polling on GPIO with configured interrupt
-  Support for asynchronous polling using `mio`or`tokio`(requires enabling the`mio-evented`or`async-tokio`crate features, respectively)

## Minimum Supported Rust Version (MSRV)

This crate is guaranteed to compile on stable Rust 1.65.0 and up.  It *might*
compile with older versions but that may change in any new patch release.

## Cross Compiling

Most likely, the machine you are running on is not your development
machine (although it could be).  In those cases, you will need to
cross-compile.  The [rust-cross guide](https://github.com/japaric/rust-cross)
provides excellent, detailed instructions for cross-compiling.

## Running the Example

Cross-compiling can be done by specifying an appropriate target. You can then move that to your device by whatever means and run it.

```
$ cargo build --target=arm-unknown-linux-gnueabihf --example blinky
$ scp target/arm-unknown-linux-gnueabihf/debug/examples/blinky ...
```

# sysfs_gpio - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/sysfs_gpio/0.6.2/target-redirect/sysfs_gpio/

## Expand description

GPIO access under Linux using the GPIO sysfs interface

The methods exposed by this library are centered around
the `Pin` struct and map pretty directly the API exposed
by the kernel in syfs [https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

Typical usage for systems where one wants to ensure that the pins in use are unexported upon completion looks like the following:

```
use sysfs_gpio::{Direction, Pin};
use std::thread::sleep;
use std::time::Duration;
fn main() {
    let my_led = Pin::new(127); // number depends on chip, etc.
    my_led.with_exported(|| {
        my_led.set_direction(Direction::Out).unwrap();
        loop {
            my_led.set_value(0).unwrap();
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));
            my_led.set_value(1).unwrap();
            sleep(Duration::from_millis(200));
        }
    }).unwrap();
}
```

[118](https://docs.rs#118)/// Flush up to max bytes from the provided files input buffer
[119](https://docs.rs#119)///
[120](https://docs.rs#120)/// Typically, one would just use seek() for this sort of thing,
[121](https://docs.rs#121)/// but for certain files (e.g. in sysfs), you need to actually

[123](https://docs.rs#123)#[cfg(any(target_os = "linux", target_os = "android"))]
[124](https://docs.rs#124)fn flush_input_from_file(dev_file: &mut File, max: usize) -> io::Result<usize> {
[125](https://docs.rs#125)    let mut s = String::with_capacity(max);
[126](https://docs.rs#126)    dev_file.read_to_string(&mut s)

[129](https://docs.rs#129)/// Get the pin value from the provided file
[130](https://docs.rs#130)#[cfg(any(target_os = "linux", target_os = "android", feature = "async-tokio"))]
[131](https://docs.rs#131)fn get_value_from_file(dev_file: &mut File) -> Result<u8> {
[132](https://docs.rs#132)    let mut s = String::with_capacity(10);
[133](https://docs.rs#133)    dev_file.seek(SeekFrom::Start(0))?;
[134](https://docs.rs#134)    dev_file.read_to_string(&mut s)?;
[135](https://docs.rs#135)    match s[..1].parse::<u8>() {
[136](https://docs.rs#136)        Ok(n) => Ok(n),
[137](https://docs.rs#137)        Err(_) => Err(Error::Unexpected(format!(
[138](https://docs.rs#138)            "Unexpected value file contents: {:?}",
[139](https://docs.rs#139)            s
[140](https://docs.rs#140)        ))),
[141](https://docs.rs#141)    }

[145](https://docs.rs#145)    /// Write all of the provided contents to the specified devFile
[146](https://docs.rs#146)    fn write_to_device_file(&self, dev_file_name: &str, value: &str) -> io::Result<()> {
[147](https://docs.rs#147)        let gpio_path = format!("/sys/class/gpio/gpio{}/{}", self.pin_num, dev_file_name);
[148](https://docs.rs#148)        let mut dev_file = File::create(&gpio_path)?;
[149](https://docs.rs#149)        dev_file.write_all(value.as_bytes())?;
[150](https://docs.rs#150)        Ok(())
[151](https://docs.rs#151)    }
[152](https://docs.rs#152)
[153](https://docs.rs#153)    fn read_from_device_file(&self, dev_file_name: &str) -> io::Result<String> {
[154](https://docs.rs#154)        let gpio_path = format!("/sys/class/gpio/gpio{}/{}", self.pin_num, dev_file_name);
[155](https://docs.rs#155)        let mut dev_file = File::open(&gpio_path)?;
[156](https://docs.rs#156)        let mut s = String::new();
[157](https://docs.rs#157)        dev_file.read_to_string(&mut s)?;
[158](https://docs.rs#158)        Ok(s)
[159](https://docs.rs#159)    }

[168](https://docs.rs#168)    /// Create a new Pin with the provided path
[169](https://docs.rs#169)    ///
[170](https://docs.rs#170)    /// This form is useful when there are other scripts which may
[171](https://docs.rs#171)    /// have already exported the GPIO and created a symlink with a
[172](https://docs.rs#172)    /// nice name that you already have reference to.  Otherwise, it
[173](https://docs.rs#173)    /// is generally preferrable to use `new` directly.
[174](https://docs.rs#174)    ///
[175](https://docs.rs#175)    /// The provided path must be either the already exported
[176](https://docs.rs#176)    /// directory for a GPIO or a symlink to one.  If the directory
[177](https://docs.rs#177)    /// does not look sufficiently like this (i.e. does not resolve to
[178](https://docs.rs#178)    /// a path starting with /sys/class/gpioXXX), then this function
[179](https://docs.rs#179)    /// will return an error.
[180](https://docs.rs#180)    pub fn from_path<T: AsRef<Path>>(path: T) -> Result<Pin> {
[181](https://docs.rs#181)        // Resolve all symbolic links in the provided path
[182](https://docs.rs#182)        let pb = fs::canonicalize(path.as_ref())?;
[183](https://docs.rs#183)
[184](https://docs.rs#184)        // determine if this is valid and figure out the pin_num
[185](https://docs.rs#185)        if !fs::metadata(&pb)?.is_dir() {
[186](https://docs.rs#186)            return Err(Error::Unexpected(
[187](https://docs.rs#187)                "Provided path not a directory or symlink to \
[188](https://docs.rs#188)                                          a directory"
[189](https://docs.rs#189)                    .to_owned(),
[190](https://docs.rs#190)            ));
[191](https://docs.rs#191)        }
[192](https://docs.rs#192)        let num = Pin::extract_pin_from_path(&pb)?;
[193](https://docs.rs#193)        Ok(Pin::new(num))
[194](https://docs.rs#194)    }
[195](https://docs.rs#195)
[196](https://docs.rs#196)    /// Extract pin number from paths like /sys/class/gpio/gpioXXX
[197](https://docs.rs#197)    fn extract_pin_from_path<P: AsRef<Path>>(path: P) -> Result<u64> {
[198](https://docs.rs#198)        path.as_ref()
[199](https://docs.rs#199)            .file_name()
[200](https://docs.rs#200)            .and_then(|filename| filename.to_str())
[201](https://docs.rs#201)            .and_then(|filename_str| filename_str.trim_start_matches("gpio").parse::<u64>().ok())
[202](https://docs.rs#202)            .ok_or_else(|| Error::InvalidPath(format!("{:?}", path.as_ref())))
[203](https://docs.rs#203)    }

[207](https://docs.rs#207)        self.pin_num
[208](https://docs.rs#208)    }
[209](https://docs.rs#209)
[210](https://docs.rs#210)    /// Run a closure with the GPIO exported
[211](https://docs.rs#211)    ///
[212](https://docs.rs#212)    /// Prior to the provided closure being executed, the GPIO
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    /// will be exported.  After the closure execution is complete,
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    /// the GPIO will be unexported.
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    ///
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    /// # Example
[217](https://docs.rs#217)    ///
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    /// ```no_run
[219](https://docs.rs#219)    /// use sysfs_gpio::{Pin, Direction};
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    ///
[221](https://docs.rs#221)    /// let gpio = Pin::new(24);
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    /// let res = gpio.with_exported(|| {
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    ///     println!("At this point, the Pin is exported");
[224](https://docs.rs#224)    ///     gpio.set_direction(Direction::Low)?;
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    ///     gpio.set_value(1)?;
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    ///     // ...
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    ///     Ok(())
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    /// });
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    /// ```
[230](https://docs.rs#230)    #[inline]
[231](https://docs.rs#231)    pub fn with_exported<F: FnOnce() -> Result<()>>(&self, closure: F) -> Result<()> {
[232](https://docs.rs#232)        self.export()?;
[233](https://docs.rs#233)        match closure() {
[234](https://docs.rs#234)            Ok(()) => {
[235](https://docs.rs#235)                self.unexport()?;
[236](https://docs.rs#236)                Ok(())
[237](https://docs.rs#237)            }
[238](https://docs.rs#238)            Err(err) => {
[239](https://docs.rs#239)                self.unexport()?;
[240](https://docs.rs#240)                Err(err)
[241](https://docs.rs#241)            }
[242](https://docs.rs#242)        }
[243](https://docs.rs#243)    }
[244](https://docs.rs#244)
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    /// Determines whether the GPIO is exported
[246](https://docs.rs#246)    ///
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    /// This function will error out if the kernel does not support the GPIO
[248](https://docs.rs#248)    /// sysfs interface (i.e. `/sys/class/gpio` does not exist).
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    pub fn is_exported(&self) -> bool {
[250](https://docs.rs#250)        fs::metadata(&format!("/sys/class/gpio/gpio{}", self.pin_num)).is_ok()
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    }
[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    /// Export the GPIO
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    ///
[255](https://docs.rs#255)    /// This is equivalent to `echo N > /sys/class/gpio/export` with
[256](https://docs.rs#256)    /// the exception that the case where the GPIO is already exported
[257](https://docs.rs#257)    /// is not an error.
[258](https://docs.rs#258)    ///
[259](https://docs.rs#259)    /// # Errors
[260](https://docs.rs#260)    ///
[261](https://docs.rs#261)    /// The main cases in which this function will fail and return an
[262](https://docs.rs#262)    /// error are the following:
[263](https://docs.rs#263)    /// 1. The system does not support the GPIO sysfs interface
[264](https://docs.rs#264)    /// 2. The requested GPIO is out of range and cannot be exported
[265](https://docs.rs#265)    /// 3. The requested GPIO is in use by the kernel and cannot
[266](https://docs.rs#266)    ///    be exported by use in userspace
[267](https://docs.rs#267)    ///
[268](https://docs.rs#268)    /// # Example
[269](https://docs.rs#269)    /// ```no_run
[270](https://docs.rs#270)    /// use sysfs_gpio::Pin;
[271](https://docs.rs#271)    ///
[272](https://docs.rs#272)    /// let gpio = Pin::new(24);
[273](https://docs.rs#273)    /// match gpio.export() {
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    ///     Ok(()) => println!("Gpio {} exported!", gpio.get_pin()),
[275](https://docs.rs#275)    ///     Err(err) => println!("Gpio {} could not be exported: {}", gpio.get_pin(), err),
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    /// }
[277](https://docs.rs#277)    /// ```
[278](https://docs.rs#278)    pub fn export(&self) -> Result<()> {
[279](https://docs.rs#279)        if fs::metadata(&format!("/sys/class/gpio/gpio{}", self.pin_num)).is_err() {
[280](https://docs.rs#280)            let mut export_file = File::create("/sys/class/gpio/export")?;
[281](https://docs.rs#281)            export_file.write_all(format!("{}", self.pin_num).as_bytes())?;
[282](https://docs.rs#282)        }
[283](https://docs.rs#283)        Ok(())
[284](https://docs.rs#284)    }
[285](https://docs.rs#285)
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    /// Unexport the GPIO
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    ///
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    /// This function will unexport the provided by from syfs if
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    /// it is currently exported.  If the pin is not currently
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    /// exported, it will return without error.  That is, whenever
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    /// this function returns Ok, the GPIO is not exported.
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    pub fn unexport(&self) -> Result<()> {
[293](https://docs.rs#293)        if fs::metadata(&format!("/sys/class/gpio/gpio{}", self.pin_num)).is_ok() {
[294](https://docs.rs#294)            let mut unexport_file = File::create("/sys/class/gpio/unexport")?;
[295](https://docs.rs#295)            unexport_file.write_all(format!("{}", self.pin_num).as_bytes())?;
[296](https://docs.rs#296)        }
[297](https://docs.rs#297)        Ok(())
[298](https://docs.rs#298)    }

[305](https://docs.rs#305)    /// Get the direction of the Pin
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    pub fn get_direction(&self) -> Result<Direction> {
[307](https://docs.rs#307)        match self.read_from_device_file("direction") {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)            Ok(s) => match s.trim() {
[309](https://docs.rs#309)                "in" => Ok(Direction::In),
[310](https://docs.rs#310)                "out" => Ok(Direction::Out),
[311](https://docs.rs#311)                "high" => Ok(Direction::High),

[313](https://docs.rs#313)                other => Err(Error::Unexpected(format!(
[314](https://docs.rs#314)                    "direction file contents {}",
[315](https://docs.rs#315)                    other
[316](https://docs.rs#316)                ))),
[317](https://docs.rs#317)            },
[318](https://docs.rs#318)            Err(e) => Err(::std::convert::From::from(e)),
[319](https://docs.rs#319)        }
[320](https://docs.rs#320)    }

[322](https://docs.rs#322)    /// Set this GPIO as either an input or an output
[323](https://docs.rs#323)    ///
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    /// The basic values allowed here are `Direction::In` and
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    /// `Direction::Out` which set the Pin as either an input
[326](https://docs.rs#326)    /// or output respectively.  In addition to those, two
[327](https://docs.rs#327)    /// additional settings of `Direction::High` and
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    /// `Direction::Low`.  These both set the Pin as an output
[329](https://docs.rs#329)    /// but do so with an initial value of high or low respectively.
[330](https://docs.rs#330)    /// This allows for glitch-free operation.
[331](https://docs.rs#331)    ///
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    /// Note that this entry may not exist if the kernel does
[333](https://docs.rs#333)    /// not support changing the direction of a pin in userspace.  If
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    /// this is the case, you will get an error.
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    pub fn set_direction(&self, dir: Direction) -> Result<()> {
[336](https://docs.rs#336)        self.write_to_device_file(
[337](https://docs.rs#337)            "direction",
[338](https://docs.rs#338)            match dir {
[339](https://docs.rs#339)                Direction::In => "in",
[340](https://docs.rs#340)                Direction::Out => "out",
[341](https://docs.rs#341)                Direction::High => "high",
[342](https://docs.rs#342)                Direction::Low => "low",
[343](https://docs.rs#343)            },
[344](https://docs.rs#344)        )?;
[345](https://docs.rs#345)
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        Ok(())
[347](https://docs.rs#347)    }
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    /// Get the value of the Pin (0 or 1)
[350](https://docs.rs#350)    ///
[351](https://docs.rs#351)    /// If successful, 1 will be returned if the pin is high
[352](https://docs.rs#352)    /// and 0 will be returned if the pin is low (this may or may

[354](https://docs.rs#354)    /// on the GPIO "active_low" entry).
[355](https://docs.rs#355)    pub fn get_value(&self) -> Result<u8> {
[356](https://docs.rs#356)        match self.read_from_device_file("value") {
[357](https://docs.rs#357)            Ok(s) => match s.trim() {
[358](https://docs.rs#358)                "1" => Ok(1),
[359](https://docs.rs#359)                "0" => Ok(0),
[360](https://docs.rs#360)                other => Err(Error::Unexpected(format!("value file contents {}", other))),
[361](https://docs.rs#361)            },
[362](https://docs.rs#362)            Err(e) => Err(::std::convert::From::from(e)),
[363](https://docs.rs#363)        }
[364](https://docs.rs#364)    }

[366](https://docs.rs#366)    /// Set the value of the Pin
[367](https://docs.rs#367)    ///
[368](https://docs.rs#368)    /// This will set the value of the pin either high or low.
[369](https://docs.rs#369)    /// A 0 value will set the pin low and any other value will
[370](https://docs.rs#370)    /// set the pin high (1 is typical).
[371](https://docs.rs#371)    pub fn set_value(&self, value: u8) -> Result<()> {
[372](https://docs.rs#372)        self.write_to_device_file(
[373](https://docs.rs#373)            "value",
[374](https://docs.rs#374)            match value {
[375](https://docs.rs#375)                0 => "0",
[376](https://docs.rs#376)                _ => "1",
[377](https://docs.rs#377)            },
[378](https://docs.rs#378)        )?;
[379](https://docs.rs#379)
[380](https://docs.rs#380)        Ok(())
[381](https://docs.rs#381)    }

[558](https://docs.rs#558)    /// Block until an interrupt occurs
[559](https://docs.rs#559)    ///
[560](https://docs.rs#560)    /// This call will block until an interrupt occurs.  The types
[561](https://docs.rs#561)    /// of interrupts which may result in this call returning
[562](https://docs.rs#562)    /// may be configured by calling `set_edge()` prior to
[563](https://docs.rs#563)    /// making this call.  This call makes use of epoll under the
[564](https://docs.rs#564)    /// covers.  To poll on multiple GPIOs or other event sources,
[565](https://docs.rs#565)    /// poll asynchronously using the integration with either `mio`
[566](https://docs.rs#566)    /// or `tokio`.
[567](https://docs.rs#567)    ///
[568](https://docs.rs#568)    /// This function will return Some(value) of the pin if a change is
[569](https://docs.rs#569)    /// detected or None if a timeout occurs.  Note that the value provided
[570](https://docs.rs#570)    /// is the value of the pin as soon as we get to handling the interrupt
[571](https://docs.rs#571)    /// in userspace.  Each time this function returns with a value, a change
[572](https://docs.rs#572)    /// has occurred, but you could end up reading the same value multiple
[573](https://docs.rs#573)    /// times as the value has changed back between when the interrupt
[574](https://docs.rs#574)    /// occurred and the current time.

[576](https://docs.rs#576)    pub fn poll(&mut self, timeout_ms: isize) -> Result<Option<u8>> {
[577](https://docs.rs#577)        flush_input_from_file(&mut self.devfile, 255)?;
[578](https://docs.rs#578)        let dummy_event = EpollEvent::new(EpollFlags::EPOLLPRI | EpollFlags::EPOLLET, 0u64);
[579](https://docs.rs#579)        let mut events: [EpollEvent; 1] = [dummy_event];
[580](https://docs.rs#580)        let cnt = epoll_wait(self.epoll_fd, &mut events, timeout_ms)?;
[581](https://docs.rs#581)        Ok(match cnt {
[582](https://docs.rs#582)            0 => None, // timeout
[583](https://docs.rs#583)            _ => Some(get_value_from_file(&mut self.devfile)?),
[584](https://docs.rs#584)        })
